name: Liquid latex (cosplay)

lead: Liquid latex is a milky emulsion of rubber particles in water. Painted onto skin in thin layers, it dries into a stretchy film that can be textured, colored and painted, which makes it a staple of costume and special-effects makeup.

Its appearance payoff is temporary and aimed at transformation: artists use it to build scars, aging wrinkles, wounds, creature skin or small prosthetic attachments for a character look. It is a costume material, not a skincare product, and no clinical studies address cosmetic outcomes.

paras: Artists brush or sponge thin coats onto the skin, often adding tissue or cotton between coats to build texture, letting each coat dry, then painting or coloring the result. It can also be used to attach lightweight prosthetics such as ears. It is removed by peeling or with product-specific removers.

Natural latex proteins can cause immediate allergic reactions ranging from hives to anaphylaxis, and additives can cause delayed contact dermatitis. About 4.3 percent of the general population is estimated to have latex allergy, with higher rates in some groups. Synthetic, latex-free versions exist. Ammonia in some formulations can irritate the airways, so ventilation is commonly advised on product guidance.

chain: Thin coats of latex applied to skin
Dries into a flexible textured film
Painted into scars, wrinkles or wounds for a character look
angle.text: Liquid latex changes how the skin surface looks for the duration of a costume or shoot. Cosplayers layer it, often with tissue, to sculpt scars, aged skin or creature textures and then color it to match the character.

lead: Liquid latex is an emulsion of rubber particles suspended in water, usually stabilized with ammonia, available in natural (from Hevea brasiliensis sap) and synthetic forms. [1] Cosplayers and special-effects makeup artists use it to create a flexible skin-like layer for wrinkles, scars, wounds, burns and other textured effects. [1]

In looks terms, it serves costume transformation: the layered film can be built up, painted and distressed to change how skin appears for a character. It is also described as an adhesive for lightweight prosthetics such as ears. [1]

Medical literature mentions liquid latex mainly in anatomy teaching, where colored latex is injected into cadaver vessels, and in latex-allergy reports; no clinical studies address its cosmetic use. [2][3]
infobox: Rubber particles in water, typically ammonia-stabilized; natural or synthetic
Scars, wrinkles, wounds, textures, prosthetic adhesive

paras: Commercial natural latex is reported to contain roughly 58 to 70 percent solids, mostly cis-1,4-polyisoprene, in water stabilized with ammonia. Synthetic versions use petroleum-based polymers such as styrene-butadiene. [1]
The film cures mainly as water evaporates, so humidity slows drying, and over-curing or heat can make the film brittle. [1]

sections.h: Use in cosplay and special-effects makeup
paras: Artists apply liquid latex by brush or sponge in thin layers, sometimes with tissue or cotton between coats, to create wounds, scars and textured effects. The dried film is flexible and can be painted or distressed to look like burns, aged skin or injuries. [1]
Latex can also hold lightweight prosthetics such as ears in place, and hypoallergenic synthetic versions are sold. [1]

Latex allergy involves immune reactions to proteins in natural rubber latex. Type I (IgE-mediated) reactions can appear within minutes and include hives, rhinitis, bronchospasm and anaphylaxis; Type IV reactions appear hours or days later as redness, blistering and itching at the contact site; and irritant contact dermatitis is a non-immune reaction. [4]

An estimated 4.3 percent of people worldwide have latex allergy, with higher rates in health-care workers and some patient groups. [4] Some sensitive people react to latex-free products made in facilities that also process latex. [4]
Product guidance cited for liquid latex mentions ventilation because of ammonia vapors, plus gloves and eye protection when handling and storage away from heat. [1]

No studies found. Liquid latex appears in biomedical papers as a colored vascular or injection-accuracy marker in cadaver studies, [2][3] and latex allergy has been documented in case reports and reviews of rubber products. [4]
